Daniel’s first idea usefully separates *economic* consumer surplus from a psychologically plausible “felt surplus,” but it hides a key assumption: that satisfaction is computed against the *best alternative you noticed*, not against your willingness to pay. That assumption sits squarely in the lineage of reference dependence and counterfactual regret—people often evaluate outcomes relative to salient foregone options rather than absolute gains (see [Kahneman & Tversky’s prospect theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prospect_theory) and [Thaler’s mental accounting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mental_accounting)). If that’s the mechanism, then “two products reduce perceived surplus” won’t be a general effect of competition; it will depend on (i) how *salient* the more expensive option is, (ii) whether the options are framed as comparable substitutes versus different categories, and (iii) whether the choice invites “I could have…” thinking. A stronger test than post-use satisfaction alone would triangulate: ask for experienced utility (usage enjoyment), decision utility (choice confidence), and regret/counterfactuals—because competition might lower *decision comfort* while leaving actual consumption largely unchanged.

The tone-sandhi experiment is more novel than it first appears, because the rolling-window manipulation targets a central psycholinguistic question: how far ahead does speech planning reach, and at what representational level does a sandhi rule apply (segment-by-segment vs prosodic chunk)? The blind spot is that a character-by-character reveal doesn’t only limit “lookahead”; it also changes reading into an unnatural production task with extra working-memory and pacing demands, which themselves can disrupt automatized phonological rules. If Daniel wants a clean inference about the time scale of 上上变调, he’ll likely need at least two controls: one that matches pacing/attention demands without removing preview (to separate “no lookahead” from “high load”), and one that varies prosodic phrasing (since many sandhi patterns track prosodic constituents, not just adjacent tones). Even a basic acoustic outcome (F0 contour on the first third tone) would make the results interpretable beyond “what they say they read,” and would connect the experiment to broader work on incremental planning in speech production rather than a one-off reading curiosity.
